thinkers.name: Masayoshi Son
thinkers.bio: Founder of SoftBank Group, owner of Arm and the SoftBank Vision Funds. He became OpenAI's largest outside financial backer (about $64.6B and roughly 13% by Oct 2026) and chairs the Stargate data-center venture.

influence: Sets a maximalist ASI narrative that others quote, but has little influence on how AI is built technically.
foresight: His long-horizon singularity/ASI dates cannot be judged yet. His dated capital calls are mixed: he exited Nvidia twice before big gains, but bet early and heavily on OpenAI.
allocation: Controls one of the largest pools of AI capital: Vision Funds, a $64.6B position in OpenAI, Stargate financing, Arm.
contribution: Commercial and financial rather than technical. He funded the infrastructure and lab buildout and owns Arm's chip IP.
corpus: Many dated keynote and shareholder-meeting statements, mostly rhetorical and with few mechanisms. Snippets often come from translated or secondary coverage.
future: His OpenAI stake and Stargate role give him substantial leverage over the frontier-lab funding cycle through the late 2020s.

mentalModel.summary: Framed AI as the coming singularity. He predicted that by 2047 chips would surpass human intelligence (a chip 'IQ of 10,000'), based on a crude transistor-vs-neuron comparison, and positioned SoftBank and the Vision Fund to ride it.

After ChatGPT he went back on 'offense'. In Oct 2023 he said AGI (10x all of humanity's intelligence) would come within 10 years and called himself nearly alone in that view, with ASI about 20 years out.
Shortened his timelines: in June 2024, ASI 10,000x smarter than humans within 10 years; by Oct 2024, AGI within 2–3 years. Said he was 'born' to realize ASI.

Moved from rhetoric to concentrated capital. He chaired Stargate ($500B over four years), committed up to $40B to OpenAI, said AGI would come 'much earlier' than 2–3 years, aimed for SoftBank to be the top ASI platform within 10 years, and sold his entire Nvidia stake to fund OpenAI.

Called AI-bubble talk 'an insult to AI' and 'blasphemy', saying AI is at the internet's early stage. Pledged to lead SoftBank for 10–15 more years to pursue ASI, and completed a further $30B OpenAI investment.

reversals.to: AGI within 2–3 years (Oct 2024), then 'much earlier' than that (Feb 2025)
reversals.trigger: Rapid LLM progress and his growing partnership with OpenAI. No specific technical trigger was stated in the sources found.

reversals.from: Large Nvidia shareholder (re-accumulated after the 2019 Vision Fund exit)
reversals.to: Sold the entire Nvidia stake (~$5.83B) to fund OpenAI
reversals.trigger: Needed cash for the $22.5B OpenAI tranche. A person familiar said the sale was not about AI valuations.

thinkers.corpusNotes: Most of Son's statements are keynote or AGM rhetoric reported through news outlets (often translated). Numbers such as '10,000x' and 'IQ 10,000' are not operationalised. The Oct 2024 '2–3 years' remark was seen only via secondary coverage of a Bloomberg report. SoftBank investments are corporate actions and are not treated as proof of his personal beliefs.

thinkers.name: Cathie Wood
thinkers.bio: Founder of ARK Invest, a thematic 'disruptive innovation' ETF manager. Its annual 'Big Ideas' reports publish some of the most quantified public AI cost-decline and productivity forecasts.

influence: Shapes retail and investor narratives about AI. Little influence on the technology itself.
foresight: The direction of her cost-decline calls was right. Her Nvidia exit (2023) and software-beneficiary calls look wrong so far, and most 2030 targets are unresolved.
allocation: Manages tens of billions in thematic ETFs. Visible but modest relative to hyperscaler capital.
contribution: No architectural or commercial contribution beyond investing.
corpus: Unusually quantified, dated annual forecasts (Big Ideas) plus frequent podcasts and posts.
future: Limited leverage over the future AI ecosystem.

mentalModel.summary: Applied Wright's Law to AI. She expected training costs to fall ~70% a year through 2030, AI software to reach up to $14T revenue by 2030 if vendors capture 10% of value created, and knowledge workers to be more than 4x as productive. She saw software and applications, not GPUs, as the next big beneficiaries, and took profits on Nvidia, calling it 'priced ahead of the curve'.
Raised the training-cost-decline forecast to ~75% a year, splitting it into hardware (~53%) and algorithmic (~47%) improvements.
Re-entered Nvidia in ARKK (April 2025). Argued the AI cycle differs from the tech/telecom bubble and found bubble worries reassuring.

Big Ideas 2026 'Great Acceleration': inference costs down >99% in a year, data-center investment rising to ~$1.4T by 2030, and real GDP growth possibly above 7% by 2030. Said the bubble is in gold, not AI.

reversals.from: Exited Nvidia entirely from ARKK (Nov 2022–Jan 2023); called it priced ahead of the curve
reversals.trigger: Nvidia's multi-year rally and the AI infrastructure buildout. Her explicit reasoning for the re-entry was not captured in sources this session.
Updated Wright's-law and algorithmic-efficiency estimates in Big Ideas 2024.

thinkers.corpusNotes: ARK forecasts are firm research products published under Wood's leadership, not always her personal words. Many figures were seen only via secondary summaries (Benzinga, iTiger, Motley Fool). ARK's '$14T' and 'AI spend' figures use broad definitions (all software spend), so they are hard to compare directly with realized 'AI revenue'.

thinkers.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
thinkers.bio: Former OpenAI Superalignment researcher who wrote the June 2024 essay series 'Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead'. It made the most-cited quantitative case for AGI by ~2027, trillion-dollar clusters, and a US–China national-security race. He then founded an AI-focused investment fund.

influence: Situational Awareness became a reference text in Washington and Silicon Valley for compute-scaling and national-security framings.
foresight: Provisional. His 2026 infrastructure checkpoints (~1GW clusters, ~$500B/yr investment) were roughly met or exceeded. The AGI-2027 and intelligence-explosion claims are unresolved.
allocation: Runs a hedge fund; reported size is uncertain and was not verified this session.
contribution: No major architectural or commercial contribution documented.
corpus: One dense, specific, dated essay series plus a long podcast. There is little dated output afterwards.
future: Influences policy framing (AGI race, lab security) more than capital or technology.

mentalModel.summary: Extrapolated 'counting the OOMs' of effective compute: compute, algorithmic efficiency and 'unhobbling'. On that basis he judged AGI by 2027 'strikingly plausible', expected automated AI researchers to trigger an intelligence explosion to superintelligence by decade's end, and expected investment to scale to trillion-dollar clusters limited mainly by power. He framed AGI as a US–China national-security contest that requires locked-down labs and a government 'Project'.

Acted through capital. He ran Situational Awareness LP, reportedly positioned in AI-infrastructure and power-related public equities consistent with the essay's thesis. No new public long-form forecasts were found this session.

thinkers.corpusNotes: WebFetch was unavailable and the search budget ran out before Aschenbrenner-specific searches, so every claim comes from background knowledge of the essay (verification 'recalled'). Numbers come from the essay's tables as remembered and should be re-checked against situational-awareness.ai. No documented public revision of his forecasts was found, and he has published little since 2024.

thinkers.name: David Cahn
thinkers.bio: Sequoia Capital partner whose essays 'AI's $200B Question' (Sept 2023) and 'AI's $600B Question' (June 2024) set the reference arithmetic for the gap between AI capex and AI revenue.

influence: His revenue-gap framing became the standard reference in AI-bubble debates.
foresight: Called the 2025 data-center construction boom. The revenue-gap thesis is neither vindicated nor falsified by Oct 2026.
allocation: Partner at a top-tier VC firm; individual allocation authority not documented.
corpus: A few influential, dated essays. Little else verified this session.

mentalModel.summary: Sept 2023: GPU capex implies ~$200B/yr of AI revenue needed, leaving a ~$125B 'hole' for each year of capex at then-current levels. AI is real but revenue lags infrastructure.

June 2024: the gap had grown to ~$600B of required revenue against ~$100B of plausible revenue (a ~$500B gap). He warned of commoditised GPU compute, lack of pricing power and fast depreciation, while saying speculative frenzies are a normal part of technology. Later in 2024 ('AI is now shovel ready') he predicted 2025 would be the 'Year of the Data Center', with booms in steel, power and construction.

reversals.from: Emphasis on the AI revenue gap and investment incineration (financial skepticism)
reversals.to: Emphasis on the physical buildout as a durable, investable boom ('AI is now shovel ready'; servers, steel and power)
reversals.trigger: Hyperscaler capex commitments and power and construction becoming the binding constraints. This is a shift of emphasis rather than a recantation; he did not retract the revenue-gap arithmetic.

thinkers.corpusNotes: Only secondary snippets were seen this session; sequoiacap.com could not be fetched. The date of 'AI is now shovel ready' is uncertain (one secondary source says July 2024). Later essays ('AI in 2026: A Tale of Two AIs'; a reported '$840B question'; a 2026 '$3 trillion question' framing) appeared only in secondary snippets with no verifiable date, so they are noted in gaps rather than used as assertions. The start date of his Sequoia role was not verified.

thinkers.name: Kai-Fu Lee
thinkers.bio: AI researcher turned investor. Author of 'AI Superpowers' (2018), which argued that China would rival or overtake the US in AI and that mass job displacement was the real threat, and co-author of 'AI 2041' (2021). In 2023 he founded the Chinese LLM startup 01.AI.

influence: 'AI Superpowers' framed the US–China AI race and the jobs debate for policymakers worldwide.
foresight: China did close much of the gap, especially in open weights. His 'age of implementation' framing underrated the LLM research and compute shift, and his job-loss horizons are unresolved but not tracking so far.
allocation: Sinovation Ventures and 01.AI; meaningful in China, modest globally.
contribution: Early speech-recognition research, founding MSRA, and 01.AI's Yi models.
corpus: Two books, op-eds, many interviews with dated numeric predictions.
future: After 01.AI's pivot away from frontier pretraining, his leverage is mostly as a commentator and investor.

mentalModel.summary: Deep learning's breakthrough was done. The next era would be one of 'implementation' and 'data', which favours China's data, entrepreneurs and state support, so China would match or overtake the US. The real danger was not superintelligence but mass job loss (roughly half of jobs within 10–15 years) and inequality.
'AI 2041' (2021) set out 20-year scenarios mixing optimism about AI benefits with concerns about jobs, privacy and inequality.
Saw generative AI/LLMs as 'AI 2.0', a platform shift, and founded 01.AI (2023) to build Chinese foundation models (the Yi series).
Argued that Chinese labs could approach US frontier models with a fraction of the compute through engineering efficiency (e.g. Yi-Lightning's claimed low training cost).

After DeepSeek, concluded that only a few giant players (DeepSeek, Alibaba, ByteDance) could keep pretraining frontier models in China. Pivoted 01.AI away from large-scale pretraining toward enterprise solutions built on open models such as DeepSeek.

reversals.from: 01.AI would build world-class Chinese foundation models from scratch (2023)
reversals.to: 01.AI stops large-scale pretraining and builds on DeepSeek and other open models for enterprise
reversals.trigger: DeepSeek-V3/R1 showed open models at near-frontier quality and low cost, while scaling costs kept rising.

Of his sources, only the NYT op-ed URL is given with confidence. The exact wording and dates of the 2017 '50% of jobs' and 2019 '40% of jobs' remarks need re-verification.

evidence.passage: Projects the largest training clusters: ~100 MW in 2024, ~1 GW (~$10s of billions) around 2026, ~10 GW (~$100s of billions) around 2028, and ~100 GW (>$1 trillion) around 2030. Total annual AI investment: roughly $150B (2024), $500B (2026), $2T (2028), $8T (2030). Power is the binding constraint, and US electricity production must grow substantially.

evidence.passage: Argues that once AI can automate AI research, hundreds of millions of automated researchers could compress a decade of algorithmic progress into about a year, leading to superintelligence by the end of the decade.
evidence.note: Conditional on AGI-level automated researchers arriving around 2027.

evidence.note: Paraphrase from memory.

evidence.title: Situational Awareness — IV. The Project
evidence.speaker: leopold-aschenbrenner
evidence.passage: Predicts that by around 2027/28 the US government will become deeply involved in AGI development through a national-security 'Project', as no startup can handle superintelligence.
evidence.note: Paraphrase from memory.

assertions.claim: The singularity, with machine intelligence surpassing humanity and improving itself, will become reality within ~30 years (by 2047), when a single chip will have an 'IQ' of ~10,000.
assumptions: Transistor counts and chip capability keep scaling exponentially
Raw hardware parity with neurons translates into general intelligence
assertions.predictedOutcome: By 2047, AI systems surpass the most intelligent humans and self-improve.
assertions.contextAtTime: Feb 2017: before the transformer paper, shortly after AlphaGo. The 2045–2050 singularity date was a Kurzweil-derived meme, not mainstream ML consensus.
assertions.outcome: Not yet evaluable. By 2026 frontier LLMs exceeded humans on many benchmarks but did not self-improve autonomously. Son himself later shortened his timelines sharply.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon is 2047. The 'IQ 10,000 chip' is not operationalised.
assertions.evolution: Shortened to AGI within 10 years (Oct 2023), ASI within 10 years (June 2024), AGI in 2–3 years (Oct 2024) and 'much earlier' (Feb 2025).

assertions.claim: SoftBank's Vision Fund disposed of its entire ~$3.6B Nvidia stake in January 2019 after Nvidia's crypto-driven share-price collapse.
assumptions: Nvidia's near-term upside was limited after the crypto bust (implied by the exit; motive also included locking in profit and Vision Fund structure)
assertions.predictedOutcome: Implied: holding Nvidia offered less value than redeploying the capital.
assertions.contextAtTime: Nvidia had fallen from ~$292 to ~$153 as crypto-mining GPU demand collapsed. Data-center AI revenue was still small relative to gaming.
assertions.outcome: Nvidia later became the defining AI-infrastructure winner. SoftBank re-accumulated a stake and sold it again in Oct 2025 for ~$5.83B.
assertions.verdictRationale: Even judged on 2019 information, Son was publicly calling AI the defining revolution, yet the fund sold the main AI-compute supplier at a cyclical low. In hindsight the exit forfeited very large gains. This is a fund action, not a statement of personal belief.
assertions.evolution: SoftBank later rebuilt an Nvidia position and fully exited again in Oct 2025, this time to fund OpenAI.

assertions.claim: AGI, which he defined as ten times the intelligence of all humanity combined, will arrive within 10 years. ASI 10,000 times smarter than humans will arrive in about 20 years.
assumptions: LLM capability gains continue to scale
'Intelligence multiple of humanity' is a meaningful measure
assertions.predictedOutcome: AGI (by his definition) by ~2033; ASI by ~2043.
assertions.contextAtTime: Months after GPT-4. Son said he might be the only person who believed AGI was within a decade, though some lab leaders were already giving similar ranges.
assertions.outcome: Not yet evaluable as of Oct 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon has not passed, and his definition is not operationalised.
assertions.evolution: Shortened within a year to 2–3 years for AGI.

assertions.claim: Artificial super intelligence, 10,000 times smarter than humans, will arrive within 10 years, and AGI (1–10x human) within 3–5 years.
assumptions: Continued exponential capability scaling
Multiple models cooperating 'like neurons' yields superintelligence
assertions.contextAtTime: Mid-2024: GPT-4o/Claude 3 era. Lab leaders were floating AGI by 2026–2030; ASI-in-10-years was an outlier claim among investors.
assertions.outcome: Not yet evaluable. At the June 2026 AGM he said he aims to achieve ASI 'in his 70s'.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon has not passed. The '10,000x' figure is rhetorical.
assertions.evolution: Repeated through 2025–2026 as SoftBank's corporate mission (top ASI platform within 10 years).

assertions.claim: AGI will arrive within the next two to three years. In Feb 2025 he revised this to 'much earlier' than that.
assumptions: Reasoning/agent models keep improving at the 2024 pace
assertions.predictedOutcome: AGI by roughly late 2026 to 2027, or earlier per the Feb 2025 revision.
assertions.contextAtTime: OpenAI o1 (Sept 2024) had just launched. Altman and Amodei were also signalling AGI-like systems in 2026–2027.
assertions.outcome: As of Oct 2026 no consensus AGI had been declared. Frontier labs reported rapid revenue growth (e.g. OpenAI ~$50–70B annualized), but definitions remain contested.
assertions.verdictRationale: The upper end of the window (late 2027) has not passed. The 'much earlier' variant is looking strained, but AGI is undefined, so it cannot be falsified yet.
assertions.evolution: Compressed further in Feb 2025 ('much earlier'). By June 2026 the rhetoric had moved to ASI 'in his 70s'.

assertions.claim: Stargate will invest $500B in US AI infrastructure over four years, deploying $100B 'immediately', with SoftBank holding financial responsibility and Son as chairman.
assumptions: SoftBank and partners can raise equity and debt at unprecedented scale
Power, sites and chips can be secured fast enough
OpenAI demand justifies the capacity
assertions.predictedOutcome: $100B deployed promptly and $500B by ~2029, with SoftBank-led multi-GW capacity.
assertions.contextAtTime: SoftBank had about $24B of cash. Musk publicly doubted the backers had the money.
assertions.outcome: By July 2025 Stargate had reportedly closed no data-center deal, and SoftBank and OpenAI disagreed over sites. OpenAI then announced ~7 GW planned and >$400B of commitments (Sept 2025), mostly with Oracle. By Sept 2026 the Oracle-built Abilene campus (no SoftBank involvement) was ~75% delivered. The SoftBank-linked Milam County site was still under construction (1.2 GW projected by 2028), and Lordstown had ~0 GW. SoftBank and OpenAI each put $500M into SB Energy in Jan 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: The 'Stargate' brand did attract hundreds of billions of commitments, but SoftBank's own capacity delivery lagged badly behind the '$100B immediately' rhetoric. Most operating capacity came from Oracle and OpenAI deals. The 4-year horizon is unfinished, so this is a mid-course partial.
assertions.evolution: No public retreat by Son. SoftBank shifted to direct OpenAI equity ($64.6B total) and SB Energy as its main channels.

assertions.claim: Concentrate SoftBank's capital on OpenAI: commit up to $40B (Mar 2025), sell the entire Nvidia stake (~$5.83B, Oct 2025) and part of T-Mobile to fund it, then invest a further $30B (completed Oct 2026).
assumptions: Value accrues to the leading frontier-model company more than to chip suppliers
OpenAI's revenue growth can justify a valuation of hundreds of billions of dollars
assertions.predictedOutcome: Implied: an OpenAI stake will outperform a diversified AI-infrastructure position such as Nvidia.
assertions.contextAtTime: 2025: OpenAI's revenue was growing fast, but it was burning cash and DeepSeek had raised commoditization fears. Analysts said the Nvidia sale was a funding need, not a bearish signal.
assertions.outcome: By Oct 1, 2026 SoftBank had invested $64.6B for about 13% of OpenAI, valued at $852B in the latest round. OpenAI's annualized revenue was ~$50B at end-Sept 2026, with ~$70B expected by year-end.
assertions.verdictRationale: The mark-to-market valuation rose, but the bet is unrealized and depends on OpenAI's long-run economics. The investment is a corporate action and not proof of a specific personal forecast.
assertions.evolution: Escalated steadily: $40B commitment, then the Nvidia sale, $22.5B (Dec 2025) and $30B more (2026). One less clearly sourced report says Son described the Nvidia sale as reluctant.

assertions.claim: SoftBank aims to become the biggest platform provider for artificial super intelligence within the next 10 years.
assumptions: ASI arrives within the decade
SoftBank's portfolio (Arm, OpenAI stake, Stargate) forms a coherent platform
assertions.predictedOutcome: By ~2035 SoftBank is the leading ASI platform provider.
assertions.contextAtTime: Post-Stargate, with the OpenAI commitment in place. SoftBank's holdings were largely financial stakes rather than operated platforms.
assertions.outcome: Not yet evaluable.
assertions.verdictRationale: Aspiration with a 2035 horizon.
assertions.evolution: Reaffirmed in June 2026, when he pledged to lead SoftBank for 10–15 more years to pursue ASI.

assertions.claim: AI is still at an early stage, and calling it a bubble is 'an insult to AI' and 'blasphemy against AI'.
assumptions: AI revenue will grow into current capex and valuations
The internet analogy holds (early skepticism, later vindication)
assertions.predictedOutcome: No AI bust: valuations and investment are justified by future returns.
assertions.contextAtTime: June 2026: hyperscaler capex heading toward ~$700B+ for the year, rising investor scrutiny, and SoftBank's own share price heavily tied to OpenAI.
assertions.outcome: Through Oct 2026 capex guidance kept rising (Alphabet, Amazon raised in July 2026) amid investor skepticism and Alphabet's first negative free-cash-flow quarter. No bust had occurred by the cutoff.
assertions.verdictRationale: This is an opinion with no horizon. Son is also heavily conflicted, since SoftBank's value depends on OpenAI.
assertions.evolution: Consistent with his 2024–2025 rhetoric.

assertions.claim: AI training costs have been falling ~70% a year (GPT-3-level training fell from $4.6M in 2020 to $450K in 2022) and should keep falling at that rate through 2030.
assumptions: Wright's-law hardware cost declines continue
Algorithmic efficiency gains compound
Cost measured per fixed capability level, not total frontier spend
assertions.predictedOutcome: The cost to reach a fixed capability level falls ~70% a year through 2030.
assertions.contextAtTime: Shortly after ChatGPT. Epoch-style algorithmic-efficiency estimates existed, but most commentary focused on rising frontier training budgets.
assertions.outcome: Per-capability costs fell sharply. ARK itself reported >99% inference-cost declines in a year by 2026, and efficient models such as DeepSeek-V3/R1 reached near-frontier quality cheaply. Total frontier training and capex spending rose dramatically (hyperscaler capex ~$700B+ in 2026).
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon is 2030. The directional trend for per-capability cost appears on track, but no independent 2026 measurement of the exact annual rate was verified this session.
assertions.evolution: Raised to ~75% a year in Big Ideas 2024 (53% hardware, 47% algorithmic).

assertions.claim: If vendors capture 10% of the value their products create, AI software could generate up to $14T in revenue and $90T in enterprise value in 2030, with software spend growing at a 42% CAGR from just under $1T.
assumptions: AI drives large knowledge-worker productivity gains
Vendors capture ~10% of value created
assertions.predictedOutcome: AI software revenue up to $14T in 2030.
assertions.contextAtTime: 2022–early 2023: AI software revenue was tiny and ChatGPT was newly launched. The figure was far above any mainstream forecast.
assertions.outcome: By Oct 2026 the two largest model vendors had annualized revenue of roughly $50–70B (OpenAI) and ~$65B (Anthropic, July 2026). That is fast growth, but orders of magnitude below a $14T end-state, and global software spend has not compounded at 42% a year.
assertions.verdictRationale: The 2030 horizon has not been reached, and the claim is conditional ('up to'). The 2026 trajectory makes the upper bound look very unlikely, but that does not falsify it yet.
assertions.evolution: Big Ideas 2026 shifted emphasis to infrastructure investment (~$1.4T by 2030) and GDP acceleration.

assertions.claim: AI should increase the productivity of knowledge workers more than 4-fold by 2030.
assumptions: Rapid enterprise adoption
AI tools substitute for large shares of knowledge tasks
assertions.predictedOutcome: Knowledge-worker output per worker more than 4x 2022 levels by 2030.
assertions.contextAtTime: Early 2023: anecdotal Copilot/ChatGPT productivity studies only.
assertions.outcome: No macro productivity surge of that magnitude was visible by 2026. Labor-market studies found little broad disruption through late 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon is 2030. The 2026 evidence points well short of the trajectory, but the claim is not falsified.
assertions.evolution: Later ARK framing moved to GDP growth (>7% by 2030) rather than per-worker multiples.

assertions.claim: ARK's flagship ARKK sold its entire Nvidia position (sales from Nov 2022, full exit Jan 2023), citing a very high valuation and profit-taking after a ~150-fold gain.
assumptions: Nvidia's valuation already reflected AI upside
Better risk-adjusted AI exposure existed elsewhere (software, Tesla)
assertions.predictedOutcome: Implied: Nvidia would underperform ARK's alternative AI holdings.
assertions.contextAtTime: Late 2022: Nvidia was down sharply from its 2021 peak and ChatGPT had just launched. The data-center AI demand surge was not yet visible in Nvidia's guidance (it came in May 2023).
assertions.outcome: Nvidia rallied enormously from 2023 onward. Estimates of ARKK's forgone gains range from >$200M to ~$1.2B. ARKK bought Nvidia again in April 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: The implied view that AI upside was priced in was contradicted within months. Her re-entry in 2025 is a tacit acknowledgment.
assertions.evolution: Re-entered in April 2025.

assertions.claim: Nvidia, at ~25x expected revenue, is 'priced ahead of the curve'.
assumptions: Nvidia's AI revenue would not grow fast enough to justify its multiple
GPUs are cyclical
assertions.predictedOutcome: Nvidia's valuation would stall or correct relative to fundamentals.
assertions.contextAtTime: Days after Nvidia's blowout May 2023 guidance, with the stock up ~172% year-to-date.
assertions.outcome: Nvidia's revenue and stock kept rising sharply through 2024–2025, and ARK re-bought in 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: Data-center revenue growth outran the multiple, so the valuation was not 'ahead of the curve' over the following two years.
assertions.evolution: Early 2024 she still called Nvidia cyclical and expectations possibly ahead of themselves (secondary, WSJ podcast; not in evidence list). She reversed in April 2025.

assertions.claim: Software providers will be the next AI beneficiaries after Nvidia: for every $1 of hardware Nvidia sells, software/SaaS providers will generate $8 of revenue.
assumptions: Platform-shift analogies (PC/internet) hold, so apps capture most value
Incumbent SaaS vendors (UiPath, Twilio, Teladoc) can capture AI value
assertions.predictedOutcome: AI software revenue becomes a large multiple (~8x) of AI hardware revenue, and the named software stocks benefit.
assertions.contextAtTime: Mid-2023: a common analogy to past platform cycles. Cahn's $200B essay (Sept 2023) would soon highlight the opposite imbalance.
assertions.outcome: Through 2026, spending stayed concentrated in infrastructure (hyperscaler capex ~$700B+ in 2026). Leading model vendors' revenue (~$50–70B OpenAI, ~$65B Anthropic run-rates) remained far below a multiple of hardware spend. Revenue accrued mainly to model labs rather than the incumbent SaaS names she cited; their stock performance was not verified this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: No horizon was given. So far the realized ratio is nowhere near 8:1 and value accrued to labs and infrastructure, which points against the claim, but it is a long-run structural claim.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: The AI cycle is very different from the tech/telecom bubble; worries about a bubble reassure her. In Jan 2026: 'the bubble today is not in AI, but in gold.'
assumptions: AI cost declines unlock demand faster than capex grows
Widespread skepticism means no euphoric top
assertions.predictedOutcome: No AI-driven market bust.
assertions.contextAtTime: Late 2025: widespread AI-bubble debate, circular-financing concerns and SoftBank's Nvidia exit.
assertions.outcome: As of Oct 2026 no AI bust had occurred. Capex kept rising, with investor scrutiny increasing (July 2026).
assertions.verdictRationale: This is an opinion with no horizon, and it is not falsified so far.
assertions.evolution: Consistent with her long-standing optimism.

assertions.claim: ARK Big Ideas 2026: global data-center system investment (~$500B in 2025) could reach ~$1.4T by 2030, and AI-driven acceleration could push global real GDP growth above 7% by 2030.
assumptions: Inference cost declines keep driving demand
Capex translates into productivity at macro scale
assertions.predictedOutcome: ~$1.4T annual data-center investment and >7% global real GDP growth by 2030.
assertions.contextAtTime: Early 2026: the IMF projected ~3.1% global growth. Hyperscaler capex guidance was rising rapidly.
assertions.outcome: Investment is tracking toward the capex part: four US hyperscalers alone guided ~$700–750B for 2026. No GDP acceleration was evident by Oct 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon is 2030. Capex is on or ahead of path, while the GDP leg is highly contrarian and untested.
assertions.evolution: Escalation of earlier ARK GDP forecasts. A secondary report of 'double-digit' GDP growth was not corroborated.

assertions.claim: AGI by 2027 is strikingly plausible: counting orders of magnitude in compute, algorithmic efficiency and 'unhobbling' implies another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump by 2027, yielding models that can do the work of AI researchers and engineers.
assumptions: Compute scaling of ~0.5 OOM/yr continues
Algorithmic efficiency gains of ~0.5 OOM/yr continue
Unhobbling (agents, long context, tool use) converts raw capability into autonomous work
No data wall
assertions.predictedOutcome: By ~2027, AI systems can substitute for remote AI researchers and engineers.
assertions.contextAtTime: June 2024: GPT-4o/Claude 3 era, before o1 reasoning models. Many researchers (e.g. LeCun, Marcus) disputed straight-line extrapolation.
assertions.outcome: Not evaluable yet. By 2026 reasoning and agentic coding models advanced substantially and labs reported very large revenue growth, but no consensus AGI or full automation of AI research had been demonstrated by Oct 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: The 2027 horizon has not passed. He hedged with 'plausible', not certain.
assertions.evolution: No public revision found.

assertions.claim: The largest AI training clusters will reach ~1 GW (costing tens of billions of dollars) around 2026.
assumptions: Investment keeps scaling ~0.5 OOM/yr
Power can be procured at GW scale
assertions.predictedOutcome: At least one ~1 GW AI cluster or campus in operation or near-complete by ~2026.
assertions.contextAtTime: Mid-2024: the largest clusters were ~100k H100s (~100–150 MW). GW-scale talk was viewed as speculative.
assertions.outcome: The Abilene Stargate campus (1.2 GW planned) was ~75% delivered by Sept 2026 per a tracker, and Epoch put it at ~0.3 GW operating in spring 2026 with completion in Q4 2026. Multiple GW-scale sites were under construction.
assertions.verdictRationale: A ~1 GW-class AI campus was largely delivered in 2026, close to his schedule. The caveat is that 'single training cluster' and 'campus' are not identical, and figures vary by source.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Training clusters will scale to ~10 GW (hundreds of billions of dollars) around 2028 and ~100 GW (a 'trillion-dollar cluster') around 2030.
assumptions: AI revenue justifies continuing ~0.5 OOM/yr investment growth
US can add ~20%+ to electricity generation
assertions.predictedOutcome: A ~10 GW cluster by ~2028 and a ~100 GW / >$1T cluster by ~2030.
assertions.contextAtTime: Widely seen as extreme in 2024.
assertions.outcome: As of 2026, the Stargate program was projected to exceed ~9 GW across seven US sites by 2029 (Epoch). That is aggregate across sites, not a single cluster.
assertions.verdictRationale: Horizons are 2028 and 2030.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Total annual AI investment will rise from roughly $150B (2024) to about $500B by 2026, ~$2T by 2028 and ~$8T by 2030.
assumptions: Revenue growth (e.g. a big tech firm reaching ~$100B AI revenue around mid-decade) sustains capex
Capital markets fund the buildout
assertions.predictedOutcome: ~$500B of annual AI investment in 2026.
assertions.contextAtTime: Big-4 capex was ~$150–200B in 2023–24. Cahn's essay the same month argued revenue would not justify even that.
assertions.outcome: 2026 capex guidance for Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta alone was roughly $700–750B, though not all of it is AI-specific.
assertions.verdictRationale: The 2026 checkpoint was met or exceeded. The later checkpoints (2028/2030) remain unresolved. The table values are recalled, hence medium confidence.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Power, not chips, will become the binding constraint on AI scaling. The US must rapidly expand electricity generation and should build clusters in the US rather than in Middle Eastern autocracies.
assumptions: Chip supply scales faster than grid capacity
Regulatory permitting is slow
assertions.predictedOutcome: Power availability and interconnection become the main bottleneck for AI data centers by the mid-2020s.
assertions.contextAtTime: Mid-2024: power was emerging as a concern (e.g. nuclear PPAs), but GPU supply was still the headline constraint.
assertions.outcome: By 2025–2026, power procurement and construction drove data-center delays and site choices (Stargate's SB Energy deals; expansions dropped or reallocated). Hyperscalers also cited memory costs and capacity constraints.
assertions.verdictRationale: Power did become a central constraint. However, chip and memory supply and financing also bound, and the policy recommendation not to build in the Middle East was not followed (not verified this session).
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Once AGI automates AI research, hundreds of millions of automated researchers could compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less, producing superintelligence by the end of the decade.
assumptions: AGI-level research agents arrive ~2027
Compute for experiments is not the binding constraint
Research progress is largely parallelizable
assertions.predictedOutcome: Superintelligence by ~2030.
assertions.contextAtTime: An intelligence-explosion argument rooted in long-running rationalist and Good-style reasoning, applied with specific compute numbers.
assertions.outcome: Not evaluable as of Oct 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: Conditional and long-horizon.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Frontier labs' security is grossly inadequate, and the CCP is likely to steal key algorithmic secrets and weights. Theft plus outbuilding on power is China's main path to staying in the AGI race.
assumptions: US labs hold decisive algorithmic secrets
Export controls constrain Chinese compute
assertions.predictedOutcome: China's frontier competitiveness would depend mainly on espionage and stolen weights rather than indigenous innovation.
assertions.contextAtTime: Mid-2024: Chinese models were viewed as clearly behind, and export controls were tightening.
assertions.outcome: DeepSeek-V3/R1 (Dec 2024–Jan 2025) reached near-frontier reasoning performance with documented indigenous efficiency innovations, published openly. US–China benchmark gaps narrowed to near parity in 2024 data. Distillation allegations arose but were not verified this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: He was right that China would stay close. His mechanism, which emphasised theft over indigenous efficiency and open publication, did not match what was publicly observed.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: By around 2027/28 the US government will launch a national-security AGI effort ('The Project'), because no startup can handle superintelligence.
assumptions: AGI progress becomes evident to national-security establishments
US–China rivalry intensifies
assertions.predictedOutcome: A government-led or government-controlled AGI project by ~2028.
assertions.contextAtTime: Mid-2024: no such program existed, and policy discussion centred on export controls and safety institutes.
assertions.outcome: Not evaluable as of Oct 2026. Stargate (Jan 2025) was a privately financed effort announced at the White House, not a government-run project.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Founded Situational Awareness LP, an AGI-thesis investment fund, after leaving OpenAI.
assumptions: Public markets underprice the AGI infrastructure buildout
assertions.predictedOutcome: Implied: AI-infrastructure and power-related equities would outperform.
assertions.contextAtTime: Launched alongside the essay and podcast in mid-2024.
assertions.outcome: Fund size and performance were not verified this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: No verified performance data. An investment is not proof of belief beyond the essay's stated thesis.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Annual GPU capex implies ~$200B of AI revenue is needed to pay it back, leaving a '$125B hole that needs to be filled for each year of CapEx at today's levels.'
assumptions: GPUs are ~half of data-center cost
End users need ~50% gross margin
Capex must be paid back by end-customer AI revenue within a short cycle
assertions.predictedOutcome: Unless AI revenue rises by over $100B a year, the capex cycle would face a revenue shortfall.
assertions.contextAtTime: Sept 2023: OpenAI was at ~$1–2B run-rate and Nvidia data-center revenue was surging. Few investors had quantified the gap.
assertions.outcome: By 2026 the two leading labs alone reached ~$50–70B (OpenAI) and ~$65B (Anthropic) annualized revenue, so the 2023-sized hole has been largely filled in run-rate terms. Capex grew several-fold (~$700B+ in 2026), so the required revenue under his method also rose.
assertions.verdictRationale: The arithmetic was a fair snapshot, and revenue did surge to roughly fill the 2023-sized gap. The framing underestimated how fast revenue (and capex) would grow, and the gap moved rather than closing.
assertions.evolution: Updated to $600B (June 2024). A secondary profile mentions a later ~$840B update.

assertions.claim: AI's $600B question: doubling Nvidia's data-center run-rate for total cost, then doubling again for end-user margin, implies ~$600B of annual AI revenue is needed. Even with generous assumptions there is a ~$500B gap.
assumptions: Same cost-stack multipliers as 2023
Revenue must come from end-customer AI products within the hardware's useful life
assertions.predictedOutcome: Absent ~$600B/yr of AI revenue, investors in the buildout face losses (he called this 'investment incineration').
assertions.contextAtTime: June 2024: Nvidia's data-center revenue was exploding while AI-native revenue was ~$10B-scale. The same month Aschenbrenner argued investment would scale to $1T clusters.
assertions.outcome: By Oct 2026 AI revenue had grown enormously (OpenAI ~$50–70B and Anthropic ~$65B annualized), but remained far below $600B. Capex kept increasing to ~$700B+ in 2026 with rising investor scrutiny. No write-down cycle had occurred by the cutoff.
assertions.verdictRationale: The arithmetic was transparent and the gap persists, but the predicted losses have not materialized or been ruled out. This is not falsified, and not vindicated either.
assertions.evolution: Later essays emphasise the physical buildout. A secondary source reports he raised the framing to ~$840B and later to a ~$3T revenue question with ~$1.5T infrastructure; not verified.

assertions.claim: The GPU shortage has subsided. GPU compute is becoming a commodity with weak pricing power, and new chips (B100) will accelerate depreciation of the existing H100 fleet.
assumptions: Supply catches up with demand
Each generation offers a large performance-per-dollar step
assertions.predictedOutcome: Falling GPU rental prices and faster depreciation of older accelerators. Compute providers lose pricing power.
assertions.contextAtTime: Mid-2024: H100 lead times had shortened and GPU rental prices were starting to fall.
assertions.outcome: Hyperscalers reported continued capacity constraints in 2026 (Wedbush on Alphabet: capacity 'remains constrained in the face of strong demand'), and memory costs rose. GPU-hour rental price declines in 2024–25 were not verified with a source this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: Commoditization of older GPU rentals likely occurred, but the 'shortage subsided' framing was contradicted by persistent 2025–26 capacity constraints as reasoning and agents drove inference demand.
assertions.evolution: Later essays turned to physical constraints (power, construction), which implies scarcity rather than glut.

assertions.claim: AI is now 'shovel ready': 2025 will be the 'Year of the Data Center', with a construction boom benefiting steel, energy (solar, batteries, nuclear) and construction, and operational challenges for hyperscalers.
assumptions: Hyperscalers follow through on capex commitments
Power and construction capacity become the critical path
assertions.predictedOutcome: A large, visible data-center construction boom in 2025, with execution and power challenges.
assertions.contextAtTime: 2024: capex guidance was rising but the physical buildout narrative was still emerging. The essay's publication date is uncertain.
assertions.outcome: 2025–2026 saw a historic data-center buildout: Stargate sites, ~7 GW planned by Sept 2025, and 2026 hyperscaler capex of ~$700B+. It came with delays, cancelled or reallocated expansions and power deals (SB Energy).
assertions.verdictRationale: The predicted boom and its physical bottlenecks materialized in 2025 as described.
assertions.evolution: Extended in later (unverified-date) Sequoia pieces noting data-center delays from power procurement and construction complexity.

assertions.claim: Speculative frenzies are a normal part of technology. Much value will be created by AI, but investors should not believe AGI-tomorrow 'get rich quick' delusions. Builders benefit as compute costs fall.
assumptions: Overbuild lowers compute costs for application builders
assertions.predictedOutcome: Some infrastructure investors lose money while application builders benefit from cheaper compute.
assertions.contextAtTime: Written in direct tension with AGI-timeline-driven investment theses such as Aschenbrenner's (same month).
assertions.outcome: Inference costs fell dramatically (ARK: >99% in a year by 2026), which helped builders. No broad infrastructure-investor losses had materialized by Oct 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: The cost-decline leg is directionally supported. The loss leg is not yet tested.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: AI could replace roughly half of human jobs within about 10 years.
assumptions: Perception and decision AI automates routine cognitive and physical tasks quickly
Firms deploy rapidly
assertions.predictedOutcome: ~50% of jobs replaced (or replaceable) by ~2027.
assertions.contextAtTime: 2017: Frey & Osborne's 47% automation-risk estimate was widely cited. Deep-learning perception gains were fresh.
assertions.outcome: Through late 2025, studies found no broad labor-market disruption attributable to generative AI. The 2027 deadline has not passed.
assertions.verdictRationale: The deadline is 2027, but the trajectory is far off. 'Replace' is ambiguous between technical feasibility and actual displacement.
assertions.evolution: Restated in 2019 as ~40% within 15 years, which lengthened the horizon.

assertions.claim: The real threat of AI is not superintelligence but mass job loss and inequality. AI wealth will concentrate in a few US and Chinese companies, and other countries may have to strike deals with them.
assumptions: AI has winner-take-most economics
US and China dominate AI talent, data and capital
assertions.predictedOutcome: AI value concentrates in a small number of US/Chinese firms, and job displacement becomes the dominant policy issue.
assertions.contextAtTime: 2017: Musk and others emphasised existential risk. Lee was contrarian in prioritising labor and geopolitics.
assertions.outcome: AI value and investment concentrated heavily in US firms (OpenAI valued at $852B; four US hyperscalers spending ~$700B+ in 2026) and Chinese firms (DeepSeek, Alibaba). Mass job displacement had not materialized by late 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: The concentration claim held strongly. The job-loss emphasis has not (yet) been borne out, and existential risk did not fade from the debate.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Within about 15 years, AI could displace around 40% of the world's jobs.
assumptions: Steady diffusion of perception and decision AI into routine work
assertions.predictedOutcome: ~40% of global jobs displaced by ~2034.
assertions.contextAtTime: Pre-GPT-3, when automation-risk studies were commonly cited.
assertions.outcome: Not evaluable. No broad displacement had been measured by late 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon is 2034.
assertions.evolution: Longer horizon than his 2017 '50% in 10 years' framing.

assertions.claim: China will match, and could overtake, the US in AI, because AI has entered an 'age of implementation' and 'age of data' that favour China's data abundance, entrepreneurs and state support.
assumptions: Data volume and implementation speed matter more than frontier research
China's consumer-internet scale translates into AI leadership
assertions.predictedOutcome: Chinese AI reaches parity with or leads the US.
assertions.contextAtTime: 2018: China led in computer vision deployment and mobile payments, while US firms dominated research.
assertions.outcome: By 2024–2026, Chinese models (DeepSeek, Qwen) reached near-parity on many benchmarks and led in open weights. The US still produced more notable models and dominated compute, capex and frontier revenue.
assertions.verdictRationale: Parity in model quality was largely achieved, but US leadership in compute, capital and frontier revenue persisted. China's catch-up was driven by engineering efficiency under compute constraints rather than data abundance.
assertions.evolution: By 2025 he emphasised that only a few Chinese giants can afford pretraining.

assertions.claim: The age of AI discovery is largely over. Deep learning was a rare breakthrough, and the next phase is implementation, where execution and data, not new research, determine winners.
assumptions: No new paradigm-level breakthroughs in the near term
assertions.predictedOutcome: Advantage shifts from research labs to implementers with data.
assertions.contextAtTime: The transformer (2017) existed, and GPT-1 and BERT appeared in 2018, but their significance was not yet widely appreciated.
assertions.outcome: The transformer/LLM scaling paradigm and reasoning RL (2018–2025) produced a new wave of discovery in which research and compute concentration were decisive. Lee himself founded an LLM lab in 2023.
assertions.verdictRationale: Judged on 2018 information, the claim was already contestable (transformers had been published). The subsequent LLM era was a discovery-driven paradigm shift.
assertions.evolution: Implicitly reversed by his 2023 'AI 2.0' framing and 01.AI's founding.

assertions.claim: Founded 01.AI to build world-class Chinese foundation models ('AI 2.0'), releasing the Yi series.
assumptions: A well-funded startup can sustain frontier pretraining in China despite export controls
assertions.predictedOutcome: Implied: 01.AI becomes a durable frontier-model developer.
assertions.contextAtTime: 2023: China's 'hundred-model war', with many startups raising funds to pretrain LLMs.
assertions.outcome: Yi-34B briefly led open leaderboards (late 2023). By early 2025 01.AI had stopped large-scale pretraining and pivoted to enterprise solutions on DeepSeek and other open models.
assertions.verdictRationale: The implied bet that 01.AI could remain a frontier pretrainer did not hold. This is an action, not a personal forecast, and the outcome evidence is Lee's own announcement.
assertions.evolution: Reversed in 2025 (pivot away from pretraining).

assertions.claim: Chinese labs can approach US frontier performance with a small fraction of the compute through engineering efficiency (e.g. Yi-Lightning reportedly trained for ~$3M on ~2,000 GPUs).
assumptions: Algorithmic and systems efficiency can offset export-controlled compute
assertions.predictedOutcome: Chinese near-frontier models trained at far lower cost than US counterparts.
assertions.contextAtTime: Late 2024: most Western observers assumed export controls would keep China well behind. DeepSeek-V3 arrived weeks later.
assertions.outcome: DeepSeek-V3 and R1 (Dec 2024–Jan 2025) delivered near-frontier performance with reported low training costs, and Chinese open-weight models became widely used.
assertions.verdictRationale: This was validated almost immediately by DeepSeek. Lee's own firm, however, was not the one to sustain it.
assertions.evolution: Led him to conclude in 2025 that only a few players need to pretrain, and that others should build on open models.

assertions.claim: 01.AI stops large-scale pretraining. China's foundation-model market will consolidate around DeepSeek, Alibaba and ByteDance.
assumptions: Pretraining costs keep rising
Open-weight leaders make second-tier pretraining uneconomic
assertions.predictedOutcome: Most Chinese LLM startups exit frontier pretraining, leaving ~3 dominant players.
assertions.contextAtTime: Shortly after DeepSeek-R1's success; China's 'AI tigers' were under funding pressure.
assertions.outcome: DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen) and ByteDance remained leading Chinese model developers. Some other labs (e.g. Moonshot, Zhipu, MiniMax) continued releasing competitive models; their 2026 status was not verified this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: The named three are leaders, but consolidation appears incomplete. The outcome evidence is thin and recalled.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

His core method ('counting the OOMs') extrapolates compute and algorithmic-efficiency scaling trends.
